claims.claim: The rostro-caudal level of the coronary artery orifice and the distribution of the arteries on the ventricles are conserved in mammals, birds, crocodiles, and lepidosaurians.
claims.source: Although the branching patterns of the vessels are diverse, the rostro-caudal level of the orifice and the distribution of the arteries on the ventricles are conserved in mammals, birds, crocodiles, and lepidosaurians (Figure 1A; Spalteholz, 1924; Erhart, 1935; MacKinnon and Heatwole, 1981; Farrell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In teleosts and chondrichthyans, the coronary artery orifices are located more cranially, branching from the hypobranchial arteries.
claims.source: In teleosts and chondrichthyans, however, the orifices are located more cranially, with branching from the hypobranchial arteries, and the arteries pass long distances from the orifices to the heart (Parker, 1886; Grant and Regnier, 1926; Corrington, 1930; May and Herber, 1957; Halpern and May, 1958; De Andrés et al., 1990; Muñoz-Chápuli et al., 1994; Icardo, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to comparative anatomy literature.

claims.claim: Coronary arteries are morphologically diverse and are frequently lost among teleosts.
claims.source: Coronary arteries are morphologically diverse and are frequently lost among teleosts, indicating that they are not essential for survival in this group, unlike in amniotes (e.g. Grant and Regnier, 1926).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Grant and Regnier, 1926.

claims.claim: Coronary arteries are not essential for survival in teleosts, unlike in amniotes.
claims.source: Coronary arteries are morphologically diverse and are frequently lost among teleosts, indicating that they are not essential for survival in this group, unlike in amniotes (e.g. Grant and Regnier, 1926).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the frequent loss of coronary arteries in teleosts and cited from Grant and Regnier, 1926.

claims.claim: In a 17.5 dpc murine fetus, two coronary arteries branch from the root of the aorta.
claims.source: In a 17.5 days post-coitum (dpc) murine fetus, the two coronary arteries branched from the root of the aorta, part of the outflow tract (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In quail at stage 28, two coronary arteries branch from the aortic root and are distributed on the ventricular wall.
claims.source: Similarly, in quail at stage 28, the two coronary arteries branched from the aortic root and were distributed on the ventricular wall (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: By 10.5 dpc in mice, the primitive coronary plexus is visible as a dotted pattern on the ventricular surface.
claims.source: By 10.5 dpc, the primitive coronary plexus was already visible as a dotted pattern on the ventricular surface.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' immunohistochemical observations shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: At 10.5 dpc in mice, ASVs form plexuses surrounding the pharyngeal arteries and one small vessel opening to the outflow tract at the root of the left branch of the truncus arteriosus.
claims.source: The ASVs formed plexuses surrounding the pharyngeal arteries and one small vessel opening to the outflow tract at the root of the left branch of the truncus arteriosus (arrowheads in Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' immunohistochemical observations shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: No vasculature is detected on the outflow trunk at 10.5 and 11.5 dpc in mice.
claims.source: No vasculature was detected on the outflow trunk at 10.5 and 11.5 dpc, indicating that the ASVs of the pharyngeal arches and ventricular primitive coronary plexus were physically separated (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' immunohistochemical observations shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The ASVs of the pharyngeal arches and ventricular primitive coronary plexus are physically separated at 10.5 and 11.5 dpc in mice.
claims.source: No vasculature was detected on the outflow trunk at 10.5 and 11.5 dpc, indicating that the ASVs of the pharyngeal arches and ventricular primitive coronary plexus were physically separated (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of vasculature on the outflow trunk.

claims.claim: By 12.5 dpc in mice, the ASVs extend from the orifice on the outflow trunk (aorta), and their peripheral end is anastomosed with the primitive coronary vessels.
claims.source: By 12.5 dpc, the ASVs extended from the orifice on the outflow trunk (aorta), and their peripheral end was anastomosed with the primitive coronary vessels (arrow in Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' immunohistochemical observations shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: In Japanese tree frog tadpoles (stage 33), a small vasculature is observed at the point of outflow tract bifurcation, with an orifice at the root of the left branch of the truncus arteriosus.
claims.source: In tadpoles (stage 33), we observed a small vasculature at the point of outflow tract bifurcation, with an orifice at the root of the left branch of the truncus arteriosus (Figure 2Ca).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: At stage 46 in Japanese tree frogs, vessels extending from the orifice are distributed on the outflow tract as truncal coronary vessels.
claims.source: At stage 46, the vessels that extended from the orifice were distributed on the outflow tract as truncal coronary vessels.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: No primitive coronary plexus is observed throughout development in frogs.
claims.source: In contrast, no primitive coronary plexus was observed throughout the development in frogs.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations across multiple developmental stages shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: In mice at 13.5 dpc, the proximal part of the ASVs degenerates and the cranial half of the aorta becomes avascular.
claims.source: In mice at 13.5 dpc, the proximal part of the ASVs degenerated and the cranial half of the aorta became avascular (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' immunohistochemical observations shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The development of quail coronary arteries is consistent with that of mice.
claims.source: The development of quail was consistent with that of mice (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' comparative observations shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: At stage 35 in quail, the arterial plexuses of the aorta and pulmonary trunk degenerate and coronary arteries are formed secondarily on the ventricular surface.
claims.source: At stage 35, the arterial plexuses of the aorta and pulmonary trunk degenerated and coronary arteries were formed secondarily on the ventricular surface.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A novel orifice is formed by an ingrowth from the connection of the ASVs and the primitive coronary plexus in mice.
claims.source: Namely, a novel orifice is formed by an ingrowth from the connection of the ASVs and the primitive coronary plexus, and remodeling results in the secondary formation of the adult ventricular coronary arteries (Bogers et al., 1989; Red-Horse et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Ivins et al., 2015; He and Zhou, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Remodeling results in the secondary formation of adult ventricular coronary arteries in mice.
claims.source: Namely, a novel orifice is formed by an ingrowth from the connection of the ASVs and the primitive coronary plexus, and remodeling results in the secondary formation of the adult ventricular coronary arteries (Bogers et al., 1989; Red-Horse et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Ivins et al., 2015; He and Zhou, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In 12.5 dpc mouse embryos, the ASV orifice is found at the root of the carotid artery.
claims.source: In 12.5 dpc mouse embryos, the ASV orifice was found at the root of the carotid artery (Figure 3Ca) and contained PECAM-1-positive endothelial cells (Figure 3Cb), as observed by confocal microscopy (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' histological observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: At the anastomosis point between ASVs and the primitive coronary plexus in 12.5 dpc mouse embryos, a vessel continues to the aorta, forming a novel (secondary) orifice.
claims.source: At the anastomosis point between ASVs and the primitive coronary plexus, a vessel continued to the aorta, forming a novel (secondary) orifice (Figure 3Cc; also see Figure 2Bc, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' histological observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: At 13.5 dpc in mice, the orifice of the carotid artery is lost and the secondary orifice becomes larger.
claims.source: At 13.5 dpc, the orifice of the carotid artery was lost and the secondary orifice became larger (Figure 3Cd).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' histological observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Endothelial invasion into the aortic wall from the ASV network at the aortic root occurs at stage 30 in quail embryos.
claims.source: In quail embryos, ASVs were more finely reticulated than in mouse embryos, making it difficult to track their pathways; nevertheless, we found endothelial invasion into the aortic wall from the ASV network at the aortic root at stage 30 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' histological observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Amniote ASVs are formed as a continuous endothelial structure from the pharyngeal region to the vascular network around the aortic root.
claims.source: These results indicate that the amniote ASVs are formed as a continuous endothelial structure from the pharyngeal region to the vascular network around the aortic root and contribute to the formation of the secondary orifice of the coronary artery.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the authors' observations in mice and quail shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: Amniote ASVs contribute to the formation of the secondary orifice of the coronary artery.
claims.source: These results indicate that the amniote ASVs are formed as a continuous endothelial structure from the pharyngeal region to the vascular network around the aortic root and contribute to the formation of the secondary orifice of the coronary artery.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the authors' observations in mice and quail shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: In breeding-aged Hyla japonica, the orifice of the outflow coronary vessels opens in the left branch of the truncus arteriosus, particularly at the root of the carotid trunk.
claims.source: In breeding-aged H. japonica, the orifice of the outflow coronary vessels opened in the left branch of the truncus arteriosus, particularly at the root of the carotid trunk (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' anatomical observations shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The topographical position of the coronary vessel in adult Hyla japonica is the same as at the juvenile stage (stage 46).
claims.source: Thus, the topographical position of the coronary vessel was the same as at the juvenile stage (stage 46; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the authors' observations at different developmental stages.

claims.claim: In Xenopus laevis at stage 54, the outflow coronary vessels are first found at the point of the outflow tract bifurcation, particularly at the root of the left branch of the truncus arteriosus.
claims.source: In the aquatic frog Xenopus laevis at stage 54, the outflow coronary vessels were first found at the point of the outflow tract bifurcation, particularly at the root of the left branch of the truncus arteriosus (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: At stage 60 in Xenopus laevis, the arterial plexus expands on the outflow tract to reach the aortic root.
claims.source: At stage 60, the arterial plexus expanded on the outflow tract to reach the aortic root.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: No blood vessels are found on the ventricular surface in Xenopus laevis.
claims.source: On the other hand, no blood vessels were found on the ventricular surface.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations of Xenopus laevis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The Japanese fire-belly newt (Cynops pyrrhogaster) has ASV-like vessels above the outflow tract, whose orifice opens into the left branch of the truncus arteriosus.
claims.source: This specie also had ASV-like vessels above the outflow tract, whose orifice opened into the left branch of the truncus arteriosus (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Frogs develop a vascular network that is morphologically similar to ASVs and is arranged directly on the outflow tract as thick truncal coronary vessels.
claims.source: These findings suggest that frogs develop a vascular network that is morphologically similar to that of the ASVs and is arranged directly on the outflow tract as thick truncal coronary vessels, whereas the ventricle has no vascular network on its surface.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their observations in multiple frog species shown in Figures 2C and 4.

claims.claim: The frog ventricle has no vascular network on its surface.
claims.source: These findings suggest that frogs develop a vascular network that is morphologically similar to that of the ASVs and is arranged directly on the outflow tract as thick truncal coronary vessels, whereas the ventricle has no vascular network on its surface.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations in multiple frog species shown in Figures 2C and 4.

claims.claim: In amniotes, blood supplied by coronary arteries enters coronary veins and is collected in one trunk, which opens into the sinus venosus.
claims.source: In amniotes, blood supplied by coronary arteries enters coronary veins and is collected in one trunk, which opens into the sinus venosus (Grant and Regnier, 1926; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Grant and Regnier, 1926 and shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In 15.5 dpc mouse embryos, the connections of the coronary artery and the vein are established.
claims.source: In 15.5 dpc mouse embryos, the connections of the coronary artery and the vein were established (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In amphibians, a vascular system distinct from truncal ASV-like vessels connects to a single tube and opens into the sinus venosus.
claims.source: In amphibians, a vascular system distinct from truncal ASV-like vessels was found in the outflow tract, which connected to a single tube and opened into the sinus venosus (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: The coronary vein is conserved between amniotes and amphibians.
claims.source: Thus, unlike coronary arteries, the coronary vein is likely conserved between amniotes and amphibians.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similar branching points and connections to the sinus venosus observed in both groups.

claims.claim: In adult flk1:egfp zebrafish (72 dpf), a peripheral network of coronary vessels is found throughout the entire surface of the ventricle.
claims.source: In adult flk1:egfp zebrafish (72 days post-fertilization, dpf), a peripheral network of coronary vessels was found throughout the entire surface of the ventricle (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Ventricular coronary arteries in zebrafish lead to the heart over a long distance directly from the hypobranchial artery, which branches off from the branchial arches.
claims.source: These ventricular coronary arteries led to the heart over a long distance directly from the hypobranchial artery, which branched off from the branchial arches (Figure 6A and B), in agreement with Hu et al., 2001.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6A and B and is consistent with Hu et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The hypobranchial artery in zebrafish bifurcates before reaching the ventricle, and its two branches extend ventrally and dorsally to connect to the vascular network on the ventricular wall.
claims.source: Before reaching the ventricle, this hypobranchial artery bifurcated and its two branches extended ventrally and dorsally to connect to the vascular network on the ventricular wall.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Vessels in zebrafish are not distributed in the walls of the outflow tract, unlike ASVs of amniotes and ASV-like vessels of amphibians.
claims.source: Unlike the ASVs of amniotes and in sharp contrast to the ASV-like vessels of amphibians, these vessels in the zebrafish were not distributed in the walls of the outflow tract.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' comparative observations shown in Figures 2, 4, and 6.

claims.claim: At the late pharyngula stage (31–38 hpf) of flk1:egfp zebrafish embryos, the Y-shaped hypobranchial artery appears in the midline of the pharyngeal region.
claims.source: At the late pharyngula stage (31–38 hr post-fertilization, hpf) of flk1:egfp zebrafish embryos, the Y-shaped hypobranchial artery appeared in the midline of the pharyngeal region, and its lateral branches bilaterally connected with the first pharyngeal arteries of the mandibular arch (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Around 36 dpf in zebrafish (juvenile stage), the hypobranchial artery is identified as a vessel running on the ventral side of the ventral aorta.
claims.source: Around 36 dpf (juvenile stage), the hypobranchial artery was identified as a vessel running on the ventral side of the ventral aorta (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: At 45 dpf in zebrafish, a vascular plexus is formed on the ventricle close to the aortic root, and part of it transiently covers the bulbus arteriosus.
claims.source: At 45 dpf, a vascular plexus was formed on the ventricle close to the aortic root, and part of it ttransiently covered the bulbus arteriosus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: At 46 dpf in zebrafish, the ventricular vascular plexus forms connections with the mid-caudal elongation of the hypobranchial artery.
claims.source: At 46 dpf, it formed connections with the mid-caudal elongation of the hypobranchial artery (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The formation of ventricular coronary arteries is complete by around 50 dpf in zebrafish, slightly before the adult stage.
claims.source: The formation of ventricular coronary arteries was complete by around 50 dpf, slightly before the adult stage.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The zebrafish does not form a novel orifice in proximity to the heart and does not lose or reconstitute the hypobranchial artery and ventricular vascular plexus.
claims.source: However, the zebrafish does not form a novel orifice in proximity to the heart and does not lose or reconstitute the above vessels.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' developmental observations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The hypobranchial artery in zebrafish is not a temporary structure and is maintained as the trunk of the coronary artery even in adults.
claims.source: The hypobranchial artery is not a temporary structure and is maintained as the trunk of the coronary artery even in adults.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations across developmental stages shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans have anatomical features similar to those of adult zebrafish, although their arteries supply the wall of the outflow tract.
claims.source: In chondrichthyans, we found anatomical features similar to those of adult zebrafish, although their arteries supply the wall of the outflow tract (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: In Lamna sp. and Narke japonica, the coronary artery originates from a vessel further cephalad than the bulbus arteriosus.
claims.source: In Lamna sp. and Narke japonica, the coronary artery originated from a vessel further cephalad than the bulbus arteriosus (outflow tract).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: In Deania calcea, the arterial trunk branches from the branchial artery, bifurcates on the conus arteriosus, and then supplies its peripheral branches to the ventricle.
claims.source: In Deania calcea, the arterial trunk branched from the branchial artery bifurcated on the conus arteriosus (outflow tract) and then supplied its peripheral branches to the ventricle.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Mice and quails have thick ventricular walls.
claims.source: Mice and quails have thick ventricular walls.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' histological observations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The ventricular wall of amphibians is spongy and thin, even in adults.
claims.source: On the other hand, the ventricular wall of amphibians was spongy and thin, even in adults.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' histological observations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Ventricular walls of lungfish and coelacanth are spongy.
claims.source: In the non-tetrapod sarcopterygians lungfish and coelacanth, ventricular walls were also spongy.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The coronary arteries of lungfish are distributed exclusively in the outflow tract.
claims.source: The previous studies suggest that the coronary arteries of lungfish are distributed exclusively in the outflow tract, like those of amphibians (Szidon et al., 1969; Laurent et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Szidon et al., 1969 and Laurent et al., 1978.

claims.claim: Zebrafish and sharks have spongy ventricles despite having ventricular coronary arteries.
claims.source: However, zebrafish and sharks, which have ventricular coronary arteries, also have spongy ventricles.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: There does not seem to be a clear correlation between the presence or absence of coronary circulation in the ventricle and its histological structure.
claims.source: Thus, histologically, there does not seem to be a clear correlation between the presence or absence of coronary circulation in the ventricle and its histological structure.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the authors' comparative histological observations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Lizard and snake hearts are spongy, yet they have amniote-type ventricular coronary arteries.
claims.source: However, Jensen et al., 2013a; Jensen et al., 2013b suggested that lizard and snake hearts are spongy, whereas they have the amniote-type ventricular coronary arteries (MacKinnon and Heatwole, 1981), indicating that the establishment of these arteries may not correlate with ventricular wall thickness.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Jensen et al., 2013a; Jensen et al., 2013b and MacKinnon and Heatwole, 1981.

claims.claim: The establishment of amniote-type coronary arteries may not correlate with ventricular wall thickness.
claims.source: However, Jensen et al., 2013a; Jensen et al., 2013b suggested that lizard and snake hearts are spongy, whereas they have the amniote-type ventricular coronary arteries (MacKinnon and Heatwole, 1981), indicating that the establishment of these arteries may not correlate with ventricular wall thickness.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lizards and snakes have spongy hearts but amniote-type coronary arteries.

claims.claim: Amniote-type ventricular coronary arteries develop through the reconstitution of embryonic vessels (ASVs) and the primitive coronary plexus, with the ingrowth formation of orifices.
claims.source: However, more recent studies have demonstrated in mice that amniote-type ventricular coronary arteries develop through the reconstitution of embryonic vessels (ASVs) and the primitive coronary plexus, with the ingrowth formation of orifices (Bogers et al., 1989; Red-Horse et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Ivins et al., 2015; He and Zhou, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: The coronary artery develops via reconstitution of primitive vessels in mice and quails, and this developmental process is unique to amniotes.
claims.source: Our present results suggest that the coronary artery develops via reconstitution of the primitive vessels in mice and quails and this developmental process should be unique to amniotes.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their comparative developmental data.

claims.claim: In frogs and newts, cardiac vessels are limited to the truncal outflow region and are composed of ASV-like vessels and the coronary vein.
claims.source: In frogs and newts, we found that cardiac vessels are limited to the truncal outflow region and are composed of ASV-like vessels and the coronary vein.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' observations shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Remodeling to ventricular coronary arteries with secondary orifices does not occur in amphibians.
claims.source: Accordingly, remodeling to ventricular coronary arteries with secondary orifices does not occur in amphibians.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of primitive coronary plexus and the persistence of ASV-like vessels in amphibians.

claims.claim: The ASVs of amniotes and ASV-like vessels of amphibians are morphologically homologous.
claims.source: Given these anatomical connections, the ASVs of amniotes and ASV-like vessels of amphibians should be morphologically homologous.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the identical topographical relationships observed in both groups.

claims.claim: In mice, ASVs contain erythrocytes and connect to the aortic endothelium.
claims.source: In mice, ASVs are considered blood vessels because they contain erythrocytes and connect to the aortic endothelium; however, a subset of early ASV endothelial cells express Prox1, Vegfr3, and Lyve1, which are markers for lymphatic vessels (Chen et al., 2014; Maruyama et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Chen et al., 2014 and Maruyama et al., 2019.

claims.claim: A subset of early ASV endothelial cells in mice express Prox1, Vegfr3, and Lyve1, which are markers for lymphatic vessels.
claims.source: In mice, ASVs are considered blood vessels because they contain erythrocytes and connect to the aortic endothelium; however, a subset of early ASV endothelial cells express Prox1, Vegfr3, and Lyve1, which are markers for lymphatic vessels (Chen et al., 2014; Maruyama et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Chen et al., 2014 and Maruyama et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Mouse ASVs have a lymphatic vessel-like identity, although they function as blood vessels.
claims.source: This suggests a lymphatic vessel–like identity of mouse ASVs, although they function as blood vessels, and their origin has been speculated to be from Prox1+ cells, which also give rise to cardiac lymphatic vessels (Maruyama et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression of lymphatic markers and cited from Maruyama et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Caecilians have a unique coronary circulation that is distinct from that of any other vertebrate group.
claims.source: Caecilians, the third group of extant amphibians, have a unique coronary circulation that is distinct from that of any other vertebrate group.
claims.evidence: This is based on cited literature about caecilian anatomy.

claims.claim: In Hypogeophis rostratus, the so-called coronary arteries supply the heart tissue directly from the trabecular spaces of the ventricle.
claims.source: In Hypogeophis rostratus, the so-called coronary arteries supply the heart tissue directly from the trabecular spaces of the ventricle (Lawson, 1966), and Epicrionops reportedly has no coronary arteries (Wilkinson, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Lawson, 1966.

claims.claim: Epicrionops has no coronary arteries.
claims.source: In Hypogeophis rostratus, the so-called coronary arteries supply the heart tissue directly from the trabecular spaces of the ventricle (Lawson, 1966), and Epicrionops reportedly has no coronary arteries (Wilkinson, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Wilkinson, 1996.

claims.claim: The coronary veins of caecilians branch from the sinus venosus.
claims.source: On the other hand, the coronary veins of caecilians branch from the sinus venosus (Lawson, 1966; Wilkinson, 1996), as observed in mice, frogs, and newts (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Lawson, 1966 and Wilkinson, 1996.

claims.claim: Caecilian coronary arteries are unlikely to be ancestral to those of other amphibians.
claims.source: We suggest that caecilian coronary arteries are unlikely to be ancestral to those of other amphibians.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the unique morphology of caecilian coronary arteries compared to other amphibians.

claims.claim: Vessels similar to ASV-like vessels have been observed in the African lungfish (Protopterus aethiopicus).
claims.source: Vessels similar to ASV-like vessels, which branch off the third pharyngeal arch artery, are distributed on the outflow tract, and end at the level of the outflow–ventricle junction, have been observed in the African lungfish (Protopterus aethiopicus; Szidon et al., 1969; Laurent et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Szidon et al., 1969 and Laurent et al., 1978.

claims.claim: The South American lungfish (Lepidosiren paradoxa) has similar vessels on the outflow tract, although their cranial part connects to the branchial arteries via the hypobranchial artery.
claims.source: The South American lungfish (Lepidosiren paradoxa) has similar vessels on the outflow tract, although their cranial part connects to the branchial arteries via the hypobranchial artery (Foxon, 1950), similar to our findings in zebrafish and shark.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Foxon, 1950.

claims.claim: Coronary arteries originating from the branchial region and crossing the subepicardium of the coronary outflow tract are shared by the actinopterygian bichir (Polypterus senegalus) and chondrichthyans.
claims.source: Coronary arteries originating from the branchial region and crossing the subepicardium of the coronary outflow tract are shared by the actinopterygian bichir (Polypterus senegalus) and chondrichthyans, although the locations of their orifices are uncertain (Durán et al., 2014; Lorenzale et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Durán et al., 2014 and Lorenzale et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The vascular connection from the pharyngeal region to the outflow tract, as seen in ASVs, is phylogenetically ancestral.
claims.source: Thus, the vascular connection from the pharyngeal region to the outflow tract, as seen in ASVs, is phylogenetically ancestral, and coronary arteries unique to caecilians are a derived trait likely associated with their heart being located near the middle of the body, which is also a derived trait.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the widespread occurrence of this vascular pattern across vertebrate groups.

claims.claim: Coronary arteries unique to caecilians are a derived trait likely associated with their heart being located near the middle of the body.
claims.source: Thus, the vascular connection from the pharyngeal region to the outflow tract, as seen in ASVs, is phylogenetically ancestral, and coronary arteries unique to caecilians are a derived trait likely associated with their heart being located near the middle of the body, which is also a derived trait.
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the unique body plan of caecilians.

claims.claim: ASV-like vessels in adult amphibians thicken to form outflow tract vessels and contain numerous blood cells.
claims.source: However, in adults, they thicken to form outflow tract vessels and contain numerous blood cells (Figure 4), indicating their function as mature blood vessels.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' histological observations shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: ASV-like vessels in tadpoles become arteries in adult amphibians.

results.result: In mouse and quail embryos, coronary arteries develop through a remodeling process involving two transient vascular structures: aortic subepicardial vessels (ASVs) in the outflow tract and the primitive coronary plexus on the ventricle. These structures are initially separated but anastomose by 12.5 dpc in mice, followed by degeneration of the proximal ASVs and formation of a secondary orifice at the aortic root, ultimately establishing the mature ventricular coronary arteries.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C20-C40 provide detailed developmental observations from immunohistochemistry, 3D reconstructions, and histological sections in both mice and quail showing the temporal sequence of ASV and primitive coronary plexus formation, anastomosis, and remodeling. The data are internally consistent across multiple developmental stages and two species, with clear visual evidence in Figures 1-3.

results.result: Amphibians (frogs and newts) retain ASV-like vessels as truncal coronary arteries throughout their lives and lack a primitive coronary plexus on the ventricle. These ASV-like vessels are distributed exclusively on the outflow tract, not on the ventricular surface, and do not undergo the remodeling process observed in amniotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C27-C29, C41-C48, C77-C78 are supported by anatomical observations across multiple amphibian species (Hyla japonica, Lithobates catesbeianus, Xenopus laevis, Cynops pyrrhogaster) at various developmental stages shown in Figures 2C and 4. The consistent absence of primitive coronary plexus and persistence of ASV-like vessels is well-documented.

results.result: In zebrafish and chondrichthyans, coronary arteries originate from hypobranchial arteries that branch from the branchial arches and connect to a ventricular vascular plexus. Unlike amniotes, these vessels do not undergo remodeling and the hypobranchial artery persists as the trunk of the coronary artery throughout life.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C53-C66, C103-C105 are supported by developmental observations in zebrafish (Figure 6) showing the formation and persistence of hypobranchial arteries from 31 hpf through adulthood, and anatomical observations in multiple chondrichthyan species. The data demonstrate that these vessels do not form secondary orifices or undergo remodeling as in amniotes.

results.result: The ASVs of amniotes and ASV-like vessels of amphibians are morphologically homologous based on their identical topographical relationships (orifices at the root of the carotid artery, distribution on the outflow tract). Amphibian ASV-like vessels represent the ancestral form of coronary arterial vessels in jawed vertebrates, while amniote ASVs are transient remnants that have been incorporated into a novel remodeling process to form true ventricular coronary arteries.
results.evaluation: Claims C79, C95, C96, C10, C9, C4 are supported by comparative anatomical data across vertebrate groups showing conserved topographical relationships. The evolutionary interpretation is based on phylogenetic distribution patterns and developmental observations. However, the homology assessment relies primarily on positional similarity rather than molecular markers or lineage tracing.

results.result: Coronary veins are conserved between amniotes and amphibians, branching from the sinus venosus in both groups, unlike the divergent coronary arteries.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52, C86 are supported by anatomical observations in mice, frogs, newts, and caecilians shown in Figure 5. The consistent branching point from the sinus venosus across these groups provides strong evidence for conservation of coronary venous anatomy.

results.result: There is no clear correlation between the presence or absence of ventricular coronary arteries and ventricular wall histological structure. Mice and quails have thick ventricular walls, while amphibians, lungfish, coelacanth, zebrafish, and sharks have spongy ventricles despite some having ventricular coronary arteries. Lizards and snakes have spongy hearts yet possess amniote-type coronary arteries.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 are supported by histological observations across multiple species shown in Figure 7 and cited literature. The lack of correlation is demonstrated by examples of species with spongy ventricles both with and without ventricular coronary arteries, though the sample size for some species (lungfish, coelacanth) is limited to single specimens.

results.result: The developmental process of coronary artery formation via reconstitution of ASVs and primitive coronary plexus with ingrowth formation of orifices is unique to amniotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C76, C75, C33, C34 are supported by the authors' comparative developmental data in mice and quail (showing remodeling) versus amphibians and fish (showing no remodeling), along with extensive citations to prior mouse studies. The uniqueness to amniotes is demonstrated by the absence of this process in all non-amniote groups examined.

results.result: The origin of coronary arteries in jawed vertebrates is defined by two vascular networks: pharyngeal vessels (ASVs, ASV-like vessels, or hypobranchial arteries) and the primitive coronary plexus. These networks have combined in various ways to produce diverse coronary vasculature morphologies across vertebrate groups. The vascular connection from the pharyngeal region to the outflow tract is phylogenetically ancestral.
results.evaluation: Claims C114, C115, C91 represent the authors' synthesis based on comparative observations across all vertebrate groups examined. The interpretation is well-supported by the anatomical and developmental data showing these two vascular components across diverse species, though the exact evolutionary relationships require further phylogenetic analysis.

results.result: Amniote-specific coronary artery remodeling may be related to morphological changes in the pharyngeal region during the water-to-land transition rather than functional requirements of the ventricle. The heterotopic shift of the heart into the thorax and elongation of the neck in amniotes resulted in reorganization of pharyngeal arch derivatives, which may have influenced the establishment of true coronary arteries with secondary orifices.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C123 present a speculative evolutionary hypothesis. While C116 is supported by the observation that lizards and snakes have spongy ventricles yet amniote-type coronary arteries (C73), the mechanistic link between pharyngeal reorganization and coronary artery remodeling (C117, C122) is speculative. The hypothesis is plausible but lacks direct experimental evidence or detailed comparative developmental data linking pharyngeal changes to coronary development.

results.result: Turtles have secondarily lost amniote-type coronary arteries, with orifices positioned in the carotid artery similar to frogs. This demonstrates that transient ASV formation is conserved during development even after acquisition of true coronary arteries, enabling evolutionary reversion. The loss may be related to peculiar shoulder girdle morphogenesis in turtles.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 are based on cited anatomical literature about turtle coronary arteries (C124) but lack direct observational data from the current study. The inference of secondary loss (C125) and the speculation about shoulder girdle morphogenesis (C127) are plausible but not directly tested. The claim about conserved ASV formation (C126) is an inference without developmental data from turtles.

results.result: Mouse ASVs have a lymphatic vessel-like molecular identity (expressing Prox1, Vegfr3, Lyve1) although they function as blood vessels, and may originate from Prox1+ cells that also give rise to cardiac lymphatic vessels. In zebrafish, the hypobranchial artery endothelium is derived from the second heart field, and mouse periaortic lymphatic endothelium overlapping with ASVs originates from Islet1-positive pharyngeal core mesoderm.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82, C106-C107 are supported by cited literature (Chen et al., 2014; Maruyama et al., 2019, 2021; Paffett-Lugassy et al., 2017). These are not original findings of the current study but represent accurate reporting of prior work on the molecular and developmental origins of these vascular structures.

results.result: The endothelial cell lineage of adult ventricular coronary arteries varies among species, even within the same class. The relative contribution of ASVs/hypobranchial arteries and the primitive coronary plexus to adult coronary arteries varies among jawed vertebrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 are supported by cited literature (Kapuria et al., 2018; Harrison et al., 2015; Shifatu et al., 2018) documenting lineage variation in teleosts and amniotes. This represents accurate reporting of prior work demonstrating developmental heterogeneity in coronary artery formation.

results.result: Caecilians have a unique coronary circulation distinct from other vertebrates, with coronary arteries in some species supplying heart tissue directly from trabecular spaces or being absent entirely. Caecilian coronary arteries are unlikely to be ancestral to those of other amphibians and may represent a derived trait associated with their heart being located near the middle of the body.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87, C92 are based on cited literature (Lawson, 1966; Wilkinson, 1996) about caecilian anatomy. The inference that caecilian coronary arteries are derived rather than ancestral (C87) is reasonable given their unique morphology compared to other amphibians and the phylogenetic position of caecilians. The speculation about body plan association (C92) is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Lungfish, bichir, and chondrichthyans share coronary arteries originating from the branchial region and crossing the subepicardium of the outflow tract, similar to ASV-like vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are based on cited literature (Szidon et al., 1969; Laurent et al., 1978; Foxon, 1950; Durán et al., 2014; Lorenzale et al., 2018) documenting coronary artery anatomy in these groups. This represents accurate reporting of prior comparative anatomical work supporting the phylogenetic distribution of ASV-like vessels.

results.result: ASV-like vessels in adult amphibians thicken to form outflow tract vessels containing numerous blood cells and constitute a network with coronary veins, functioning as mature arteries.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by histological observations in adult amphibians shown in Figure 4, demonstrating that these vessels are functional blood vessels rather than transient embryonic structures. The connection with coronary veins provides evidence for their arterial function.

results.result: Amniote ASVs have probably lost their arterial function but may be maintained as embryonic primordia for subsequent development, representing an example of developmental burden.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 are speculative interpretations. While the transient nature of ASVs in amniotes is well-documented, the claim that they are maintained as developmental burden (citing Riedl, 1978; Fujimoto et al., 2022) is a theoretical framework rather than a directly tested hypothesis. The functional status of ASVs during their brief existence is not definitively established.

results.result: Anomalous coronary arteries originating from the brachiocephalic artery in humans can be considered persistent embryonic vasculature similar to ASVs, as the brachiocephalic artery is derived from the third pharyngeal arch artery.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 are supported by cited clinical literature (Davis and Lie, 1977; Asada et al., 2019; Pandey et al., 2019; Santucci et al., 2001; Duran et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2009) documenting these anomalies. The interpretation that these represent persistent ASVs (C131) is a reasonable inference based on the anatomical similarity and developmental origin, though direct developmental evidence is not provided.

results.result: Coronary arteries provide nourishment to the heart, and in humans, even minor defects can be lethal due to coronary artery disease caused by atherosclerosis and thrombosis, indicating that ventricular coronary arteries are essential for human survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C11, C12 represent established medical knowledge supported by cited literature (Nabel and Braunwald, 2012; Khera and Kathiresan, 2017). These are background claims providing context for the importance of coronary arteries in humans.

results.result: Some teleosts survive without coronary arteries, which are morphologically diverse and frequently lost in this group, indicating they are not essential for survival in teleosts unlike in amniotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C18, C19 are supported by cited literature (Grant and Regnier, 1926) documenting the variable presence of coronary arteries in teleosts. This represents established comparative anatomical knowledge providing evolutionary context.

results.result: Coronary circulation is completely absent in cyclostomes (lampreys and hagfishes), and the coronary artery is generally considered a synapomorphy of jawed vertebrates, though whether the absence in cyclostomes is ancestral or a secondary loss is uncertain.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C14, C128 are based on cited literature (Grant and Regnier, 1926) documenting the absence of coronary circulation in cyclostomes. This represents established comparative anatomical knowledge, though the uncertainty about ancestral vs. derived absence (C128) is appropriately noted.

results.result: In humans and other amniotes (mammals, birds, crocodiles, lepidosaurians), coronary artery orifices are located at the aortic sinuses close to the ventricle with arteries distributed on the ventricular surface. In teleosts and chondrichthyans, orifices are located more cranially, branching from hypobranchial arteries.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 represent established comparative anatomical knowledge supported by multiple citations (Spalteholz, 1924; Erhart, 1935; MacKinnon and Heatwole, 1981; Farrell et al., 2012; Parker, 1886; Grant and Regnier, 1926; and others) and illustrated in Figure 1A. This provides the anatomical foundation for the study.

results.result: Fish hearts are classified into four types based on coronary artery distribution. The lack of extrinsic cardiac circulation in some teleosts is a derived trait. Some chondrichthyans and amniotes have posterior coronary arteries (conus arteries) branching from subclavian arteries.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are based on cited literature (Tota et al., 1983; Tota, 1989; Icardo, 2017; De Andrés et al., 1990; Farrell et al., 2012; Durán et al., 2014; Farrell and Smith, 2017; Lorenzale et al., 2018; Muñoz-Chápuli et al., 1994; Schlesinger et al., 1949; Simons, 1965) documenting the diversity of fish coronary systems. This represents accurate reporting of prior comparative work.

results.result: The coronary arteries of lungfish are distributed exclusively in the outflow tract, like those of amphibians.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is based on cited literature (Szidon et al., 1969; Laurent et al., 1978). While the authors could not directly observe coronary arteries in their lungfish specimen due to limited resolution (Figure 7), the cited literature provides support for this anatomical description.

results.result: The ventricular coronary artery of adult amniotes originated through ancestral cardiovascular remodeling during the evolution of amniotes.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 represents the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing all the comparative anatomical and developmental data. It is well-supported by the demonstrated presence of remodeling in amniotes (mice, quail) and its absence in non-amniotes (amphibians, fish), along with the homology of ASVs across groups. However, the term 'ancestral cardiovascular remodeling' could be clearer—it refers to a novel remodeling process that arose in the amniote ancestor, not remodeling of an ancestral state.
